answer.answer:
**Summary**

To adopt robotic assembly you have to change the delivery arrangement itself, not just procure the machine: the business model, contracting route and work culture are a stated precondition, backed by peer-reviewed evidence [1]. Two concrete changes travel with that: the work has to be fed by extensive prefabrication and unification of materials, and the party that will actually produce and assemble has to be brought into design early enough for a delivery method that permits it. Alongside those, plan for workforce skills and training, for a highly detailed definition of tasks if you intend to run short takt, and for compliance with robot safety standards wherever people work beside the machines. Watch one gap: the deployed Japanese records in front of me, several of them assembly processes at high readiness, are not linked to the delivery/business-model enabler, so this requirement rests on the literature rather than on a coded deployment.

**Detailed answer**

**The delivery model is a named requirement, not a by-product**

Robotic assembly (PR4) depends on the delivery/business model/work culture enabler (RI12), on the grounds that robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [1] (DEP61, peer-reviewed [1]). This is a directional dependency, not a correlation: the delivery arrangement is upstream of the robotic process.

RI12 carries exactly two inbound dependency edges and no outbound ones, and both are listed, so the pair can be quoted as complete: DEP61 from robotic assembly, and DEP81, where adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale (AT8) depends on adapted business models [2] [2]. In other words, the delivery model is invoked at two scales, the individual robotic assembly process and the move to industrialised scale, and nothing in the graph has the delivery model in turn depending on something else. RI12 is activated in 16 of the 50 coded cases [2], and PR4 in 13 [2].

**What changes concretely, within PR4's complete edge set**

PR4 carries 4 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges, all listed [2], so the following is the full requirement picture for robotic assembly here:

- Feedstock and standardisation. Robotic assembly has prefabrication (PR2) as a precondition: automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [2] (DEP55) [3], and Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components [2] (DEP88, AT7) [4].
- Equipment and planning. A robot arm (RE2) is required [2] (DEP24) [5], and path planning (PR12) is a precondition for robotic assembly [2] (DEP23) [6].
- Site conditions. All-weather cover (CO12) allows welding and assembly to proceed in a normal manner even in rain [2] (DEP42) [7].
- What you get back. Robotic and factory assembly reduces errors, a quality-control gain (VA10) [2] [8], and it amplifies productivity (VA2) and economic benefit (VA6), productivity being higher when the robotic method is used for geometrically complex walls [2] [9].

**Contracting route: the production party in early design**

The clearest delivery-procedure change sits on early contractor involvement (CO11): integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party, manufacturer, fabricator or contractor, to be involved in the early design phase, and a project delivery method that involves participants in early design should be selected [2] (DEP22, enabling prefabrication PR2) [10]. The same enabler feeds integrated design-DFAB adoption, where BIM and early contractor involvement improve design management and increase adoption [2] (DEP65) [11]. CO11 is activated in 14 of the 50 coded cases [2]. Organisationally, integrated design-DFAB processes (AT12) have vertical integration as a precondition, because technically interdependent systems require tighter organisational coupling such as a single firm [2] (DEP35) [12].

**People, safety and takt**

Human-robot collaboration (CO6) depends on addressing workforce training (RI6), since its success is contingent on a skilled workforce [2] (DEP34) [13], and it depends on compliance with robot safety standards [2] (DEP45, standard-grade evidence [14]); power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigates contact-injury risk [2] (DEP57) [15]. CO6 is activated in 32 of the 50 coded cases [2]. The same training requirement reappears on AR9, where high sophistication of digital technologies prohibits adoption by less technologically familiar workers [2] (DEP100) [16]. On scheduling, short-takt production requires a highly detailed definition of tasks to avoid ambiguousness [2] (DEP99) [17]; AR14 is activated in 28 of the 50 coded cases [2].

**The deployed record**

The census records retrieved here show the robotic processes in service but do not, in this context, carry enabler links, so none of them can be said to activate RI12.
